_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version, from latent-season9-bible-v1.0.0.md row a9e06 and writer brief a9e06-v1.0.0.md. a9e05's next field was honoured: AI product sense, when AI is the wrong tool, designing for uncertainty and trust. Keeps apart from s9e11 (whether a model belongs in the path, not which service to run), a6e08 (no printing presses, no prompt versioning) and the craft-workshop cases (the order form, the proof and the plate, not workshop craft). Timeline: the tidy step was tested and went live on Monday 14 September 2026 (200 test lines, 15 typos, 14 fixed, 0 of 185 correct lines changed, not counted until 00:20 on Friday 11 December); since then 40 jobs and 310 plates, before the club's job. The club's job is job 41: 120 lines typed on Friday 4 December, proof sent Saturday 5 December, approved at 16:02 on Monday 7 December with the secretary's email; the tidy step ran on the 120 lines at 16:03 and saved the plate file; engraved Thursday 10 December, 18:00 to 22:40; 23:10 the email reread; 23:15 to 00:15 the compare (9 lines differ: 3 typos fixed, 6 of 117 correct names changed, 6 × £8 = £48); post at about 00:30 on Friday 11 December; presentation night Saturday 12 December, collection 17:00. The 120 lines are not among the 310 plates. Checking time: 30 seconds a line, 60 minutes per 120 lines, doubled to 120 by staff compare. Replies play from the 00:30 post. Cold case: 3 months later, Monday 14 December to Wednesday 10 March 2027. Sources read 16 October 2026; the Amershi et al. guidelines are named, not quoted, because their wording could not be checked in the paper's PDF; only the abstract's first sentence is quoted.
title: The Wrong Tool

post.author: u/proof_to_plate_duarte
post.title: I added a tidy step to my family's engraving shop. On Thursday, plate 47 for a swimming club came off the machine reading 'Kristopher'. The proof the club approved says 'Kristoffer'.

blocks.text: By day I'm a junior AI engineer: I build software that uses AI models. In December I help at my family's trophy and engraving shop, where an engraving machine cuts the words into brass plates. It's our busiest week: presentation nights, club cups, and long-service plaques from firms.

An order runs in steps. First, the customer types each plate's words into the order form on our website, one line per plate. Next, we send a proof: a picture of every plate, made from that text, for the customer to check.

Then the customer clicks approve, and that wording becomes the approved text. Last, the machine reads a file of the lines, one per plate, and cuts each line exactly as written. That file is the plate file.

Customers' own typos cost us £8 a plate to cut again. So in September I added a step between approval and the machine. It uses a language model: a program that has read huge amounts of text and writes the likeliest words for what it's given, like autocorrect on a phone. I call it the tidy step.

It works in three steps. It reads the approved text a line at a time. It writes each line back the way its instructions, the standing orders sent with every list, tell it: fix capitals, double spaces and obvious typos. Then it saves the result as the plate file. Its changes, my tidy-ups, go straight to the machine.

On Monday 14 September I tested it on 200 lines from last year's orders, 15 with typos. It fixed 14. I never counted what it did to the other 185, the correct ones. Then I switched it on. Since then: 40 jobs, 310 plates, mostly long-service plaques with names from firms' payroll lists. No complaints.

Job 41 was a swimming club's presentation night, Saturday 12 December: 120 plates, each a swimmer's first name and an award. The club secretary typed the lines on Friday 4 December, and we sent the proof on Saturday. She approved it at 16:02 on Monday 7 December, with an email I skimmed. At 16:03 the tidy step ran on her 120 lines and saved the plate file.
On Thursday I engraved all 120, from 18:00 to 22:40. Each line of the machine's log shows the time, what it did, and the result:

18:02  read plate_file_club   120 lines
19:51  cut plate 47           as in file
22:40  job done               120 of 120 as in file
At 23:10 I reread her Monday email, looking for the collection time. Under 'Approved, thank you' was a line I had skimmed:
Please double-check Kristoffer, everyone gets it wrong.
Plate 47 reads Kristopher. The proof she approved says Kristoffer. From 23:15 to 00:15 I compared every line of the plate file with the proof. Nine lines differ.

blocks.title: Plate file against the approved proof, all 120 lines
items: 3 real typos, fixed: butterfy to butterfly, freestlye to freestyle, breastsroke to breaststroke.
6 correct names, changed: Kristoffer to Kristopher, Katelynn to Katelyn, Zoë to Zoe, Rebekah to Rebecca, Jaden to Jayden, Leyton to Layton.

blocks.text: So 6 of the 117 correct lines were changed, each name into a commoner spelling. Six plates to cut again before Saturday: 6 × £8 = £48, and Friday night. My test lines and the plaques held common spellings. This list didn't.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in that shop is haunted, and the machine did its job. Your tidy step writes the likeliest spelling of each line. A rare spelling is unlikely by definition, so to it 'Kristoffer' and 'butterfy' look the same: something to fix. A count also needs its denominator, the number it is out of: you counted fixes out of 15 typos and nothing out of 185 correct lines. There's an interview round for nights like this. It's called the product sense round, and a favourite question there is when you would not use AI at all. Two questions. Which document did the secretary actually say yes to? And when the tidy step changes a line, who sees it before the brass does?

replies.author: u/proof_to_plate_duarte
replies.text: She said yes to the proof, made from her own typing, three typos and all. Nobody sees a change: the file goes from the tidy step straight to the machine. My compare took an hour for 120 lines, as long as our check of each proof before it goes out.

comments.author: u/clean_plates_thiago
comments.text: It fixed 14 of 15 typos and 310 plates went out clean; six odd names is the price. Before September every customer typo cost you £8, and nobody thanks you for the ones you caught. Don't rip it out over one swimming club. Put a bigger model behind it, one that has read more names, and it will know Kristoffer.

replies.author: u/proof_to_plate_duarte
replies.text: Tonight's list: 3 typos fixed, 6 of 117 correct names changed. The 310 were mostly payroll names.

comments.author: u/sure_enough_ugochi
comments.text: Keep the fixes, lose the guesses. Ask the tidy step for a sureness score with each change: how sure it is, from 0 to 100%. Then set a 90% sure rule, so it changes only what scores 90 or more. A typo like freestlye is obvious; a name it hasn't met should score low.

replies.author: u/proof_to_plate_duarte
replies.text: I asked it to score Monday's 9 changes. The typos: 99, 98, 97. The names: Zoë 97, Kristoffer 94, Katelynn 92, Leyton 91, Rebekah 86, Jaden 83.

reply.prompt: It's 00:30 on Friday 11 December. The club collects at 17:00 on Saturday, and more lists come next week. What should I change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Engrave the approved text exactly; offer tidy-ups before the proof.
options.part2: On Friday morning I took the tidy step out of everything after approval. The plate file is now the approved text, letter for letter, and the machine cuts that. From 18:00 I cut the six plates again from the proof, Kristoffer, Katelynn, Zoë, Rebekah, Jaden and Leyton: £48. Then I moved the tidy step before the proof. Its changes now go to the customer as suggestions, the changed letters highlighted, and the customer accepts or rejects each line; the proof is made from what they chose. In the sim I replayed the club's list that way: 9 suggestions, the secretary accepts the 3 typo fixes and rejects the 6 name changes, 120 of 120 plates match the approved proof, £0 to cut again, and checking still takes 60 minutes. It went live on Monday 14 December. On Saturday night the secretary sent a photo of plate 47.
options.senior: After approval, a plate has one right answer: the approved text, letter for letter. A model that writes likely text adds nothing there and can only move away from it, and rare names are where it moves. Before approval it can help, as long as it suggests, shows what it changed, and lets a person decide each line. The model stays where being wrong costs a click, and leaves the place where being wrong costs a plate and a swimmer's name.

options.text: Use a bigger model that knows more names, so it stops changing them.
options.part2: On Friday I switched the tidy step to a bigger model and replayed Monday's list in the sim before cutting anything. It left Katelynn, Rebekah and Jaden alone and still changed Zoë to Zoe, Kristoffer to Kristopher and Leyton to Layton: 3 of 117 correct names wrong, 114 of 120 plates matching the proof, and £24 to cut again had that been the real night. Nobody would have seen any of the three before the machine did. I cut the six plates again from the proof for £48 and wondered how many names next week's lists hold that no model has read.
options.senior: A bigger model knows more spellings, so it makes fewer of these changes, but it still writes the likeliest text, and a rare name is still unlikely. It cannot tell a rare name from a typo; it can only know more of them. Each failure is now rarer and just as silent, which makes it harder to find. Making the model better doesn't answer the real question: should any model touch the approved text?

options.text: Add 'never change names' to the tidy step's instructions right away.
options.part2: At 00:40 I added 'never change names' to its instructions and replayed Monday's list in the sim. The three typos were still fixed. Four names were left alone, but Zoë still became Zoe and Leyton still became Layton: 2 of 117 correct names wrong, 115 of 120 plates matching the proof, £16 had it been the real night. To the tidy step, the dots on Zoë and the spelling of Leyton looked like typos, not names. Nobody would have seen those two before the brass either. I cut the six plates again for £48.
options.senior: Instructions are a request a model usually follows, not a guarantee. And this one asks the model to know which words are names, which is the very thing it cannot tell: a rare name looks like a typo to it. The count goes down and the changes stay silent. When a job needs 'never', put it in the design, by keeping the model out of that path, not in the wording sent to the model.

options.text: Have staff compare every plate file with its proof before engraving.
options.part2: From Friday, staff compare every line of each plate file with its proof before the machine reads it. Replayed in the sim on the club's list, the compare caught all 9 differences: the 6 names went back to the proof's spelling and the 3 typo fixes stayed. 0 of 117 names wrong and £0 to cut again, though 3 of 120 plates now differ from the proof on purpose, the typo fixes kept, and checking 120 lines takes 120 minutes, not 60, in the busiest week of the year. The tidy step still changes approved text; staff are now paid to undo it.
options.senior: Checking every output catches every silent change, and where a model must stay after approval it is the safe minimum. But it doubles the checking, and it keeps a step whose changes have to be found and undone. The cheaper design moves the model to where its changes are seen anyway, before the proof, and leaves nothing to compare after approval.

sim.title: Compare every plate with its proof
sim.lede: You're the engraver's son on Monday 14 September 2026, with the tidy step's test sheet on the bench. No real model runs here: every change the tidy step makes is given data. Given: the test, 200 lines from last year's orders, 185 correct with common spellings and 15 with typos; it fixed 14 and left 'sliver medal', a real word. The club's list: 120 lines numbered by plate, approved at 16:02 on Monday 7 December, run through the tidy step at 16:03. 111 are correct with common spellings, 6 are correct rare names (12 Katelynn, 29 Zoë, 47 Kristoffer, 63 Rebekah, 88 Jaden, 105 Leyton) and 3 have typos in award words (8 butterfy, 54 freestlye, 97 breastsroke). The tidy step changes all 9, each name into a commoner spelling, and gives each change a sureness score: typos 99, 98, 97; Zoë 97, Kristoffer 94, Katelynn 92, Leyton 91, Rebekah 86, Jaden 83. A bigger model still changes Zoë, Kristoffer and Leyton. With 'never change names' in its instructions it still changes Zoë and Leyton. The 90% sure rule changes only what scores 90 or more. Before the proof, the secretary accepts the 3 typo fixes and rejects every name change. Staff compare puts back every changed name and keeps the typo fixes. A plate cut again costs £8. Staff check each proof at 30 seconds a line, 60 minutes for 120 lines; a compare of the plate file takes the same again.
sim.tryThis: Try this: step the moment. September: 14 of 15 typos fixed, and 0 of 185 correct lines changed, the count nobody looked at. 16:03 Monday: 9 of 120 lines changed after approval. 23:10: plate 47 reads Kristopher. The compare: 6 of 117 names wrong, 111 of 120 plates match, 6 × £8 = £48. Now move the tidy step before the proof: 9 suggestions, 3 accepted, 120 of 120 match. Switch it off: 3 typos cut, £24. Back after approval, try the bigger model (3 of 117), 'never change names' (2 of 117) and the 90% sure rule (4 of 117). Turn on staff compare: 0 of 117, checking 120 minutes. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the shop was haunted. The tidy step sat after approval and wrote the likeliest spelling of every line into the plate file. To it, a rare name and a typo look the same, so it fixed 3 typos and changed 6 of 117 correct names, and nobody saw the file before the machine cut it.

steps.title: What the tidy step did, step by step.
steps.text: First, the secretary approved the proof at 16:02 on Monday. Next, at 16:03, the tidy step read each approved line and wrote back the likeliest version of it. Then it saved those lines as the plate file. Last, on Thursday, the machine cut exactly that file. What can go wrong: at the second step a language model writes likely text (a1e06 met it as next-word guessing), and a rare spelling is unlikely by definition, so Kristoffer looked to it just like butterfy: something to fix. 3 typos fixed, 6 correct names changed, 9 lines in all, and no person saw one of them.

steps.title: Why the test said 14 of 15.
steps.text: The September test counted fixes out of 15 typo lines and nothing out of the 185 correct ones. A count without its denominator hides the other half: the question was also how many of the 185 it changed. It changed 0 of 185, because last year's lines, like the payroll plaques, held common spellings. The club's list held 6 rare ones, so 6 of 117. What can go wrong: a test drawn from easy cases passes a step that fails on the first hard list.

steps.title: One right answer is the wrong job for a likely-text writer.
steps.text: After approval there is exactly one right plate: the approved text, letter for letter. A model that produces likely text adds nothing there; it can only match it or move away from it. Google's People + AI Guidebook lists predictability and costly errors among the cases where AI is probably not better, and a swimmer's name cut wrong on presentation night is a costly error. Patrick McKenzie's list of falsehoods about names includes the belief that names which break your system are weird outliers. What can go wrong: 'usually right' sounds like a feature, but this job only rewards 'always'.

steps.title: Suggest, show, let a person decide.
steps.text: The model is still useful before the proof: a customer who typed butterfy wants to be told. So it suggests: each change shown with the changed letters highlighted, and the customer accepts or rejects it line by line. Then the proof is made from what they chose, and the machine cuts that exactly. This is a4e07's ask before you act, placed where the person still holds the pen. And a2e03's lesson applies too: a plate file in a fixed shape, one line per plate, says nothing about whether its words are right. What can go wrong: a suggestion accepted without reading is a silent change with a signature.

steps.title: Trust is lost faster than it is earned.
steps.text: Customers don't notice 3 fixed typos; they notice one swimmer's name spelled wrong on presentation night. A bigger model changed 3 of 117 names, the instruction 2, the 90% sure rule 4: each fewer, none zero, all silent. Staff comparing every plate file catches all 6 but doubles checking from 60 to 120 minutes. Taking the model out of the path after approval makes the count 0 by design. Dead Letter's s9e11, Build or Buy, asks which service to run; this case asks whether a model belongs in the path at all. What can go wrong: improving the model makes the failures rarer and harder to see.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn as a flow. Top row: the order form, where the customer types the lines; tidy suggestions with the changed letters highlighted, 9 on the club's list; the customer decides, accepting or rejecting each, 3 kept and 6 rejected; the proof, made from what they chose. A bent line takes the proof down to the bottom row: approval, the approved text; the plate file, the approved text letter for letter; the engraving machine cuts the file; 120 plates, 120 of 120 matching, £0 to cut again. A note: no model between approval and the machine.

notes.text: No model between approval and the machine

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right: the tidy step works before the proof, as suggestions the customer accepts or rejects line by line. The bent line is the proof going for approval. Bottom row: from approval on there is no model; the plate file is the approved text, letter for letter, and the machine cuts exactly that.

fix.title: The fix: the approved text, exactly; the tidy-ups before the proof
fix.text: Take the model out of everything after approval: the plate file is the approved text, letter for letter, and the machine cuts that. Move the tidy step before the proof, as suggestions: each change shown with its changed letters highlighted, and the customer accepts or rejects it line by line. Make the proof from what they chose. On the club's list that is 9 suggestions, 3 typo fixes accepted and 6 name changes rejected, 120 of 120 plates matching the approved proof, £0 to cut again, and checking still about 60 minutes. Tonight, cut the six plates again from the proof, £48, and tell the secretary what happened.

limits: Suggestions only help if they are read. A customer who accepts every suggestion without looking turns it back into a silent change with a signature, so keep the customer's own text as the default.

The test still needs its other half: run the tidy step on correct lines with rare spellings and count what it changes out of all of them, not only fixes out of typos. One club's list is a small sample: 6 of 117 might be 3 or 10 on another list.
Typos the customer misses on the proof are still cut, as before September, and some £8 plates will still be engraved again. That is the price of engraving exactly what was approved.

explain.seniorTake: Before asking which model, ask whether the job wants a model at all. After approval a plate has one right answer, the approved text letter for letter, and a model that produces likely text can only match it or move away from it. Rare names are where it moves, because rare means unlikely, and to the model a rare name and a typo look the same. Count both halves with their denominators: 14 of 15 typos fixed said nothing about 6 of 117 correct names changed. A model that can be wrong should suggest, show what it changed and let a person decide, before the approval, not after it. A bigger model, a firm instruction or a 90% cut-off each shrink the count and keep it silent; staff checking every plate catches it at twice the time. One silent change on presentation night loses more trust than a year of fixed typos earns. In interviews, the product sense round tests exactly this: expect 'when would you not use a language model?'

realWorld.title: Google PAIR: when predictability is the product
realWorld.text: The People + AI Guidebook's chapter User Needs + Defining Success lists situations where AI is probably not better. One is Maintaining predictability: Sometimes the most valuable part of the core experience is its predictability, regardless of context or additional user input. A plate's core experience is the approved text, every time.

realWorld.title: Google PAIR: when errors cost more than they save
realWorld.text: The same list includes Minimizing costly errors: If the cost of errors is very high and outweighs the benefits of a small increase in success rate, such as a navigation guide that suggests an off-road route to save a few seconds of travel time. Three typos fixed did not outweigh six names cut wrong.

realWorld.title: McKenzie, 2010: names that break your system
realWorld.text: Patrick McKenzie's Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names, originally written on 16 June 2010, lists among the falsehoods: People whose names break my system are weird outliers. Six of the club's 117 correct lines were that kind of name.

realWorld.title: Amershi and colleagues, CHI 2019: guidelines for human-AI interaction
realWorld.text: Microsoft researchers' paper Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction says: We propose 18 generally applicable design guidelines for human-AI interaction. It is named here for further reading; its guidelines are not quoted, because their wording was not checked in the paper itself.

asked: When would you not use a language model?
A model fixes 14 of 15 typos in your test. Would you ship it?
interview.answer: When the job has one known right answer that must be copied exactly, and a wrong one is costly. In a shop I helped, a model tidied customers' plate text after they approved it. In its test it fixed 14 of 15 typos, and nobody counted what it did to the 185 correct lines. On a swimming club's list it fixed 3 typos and changed 6 of 117 correct names into commoner spellings, because to a model that writes likely text a rare name and a typo look the same. So first I'd ask for every count with its denominator, including what it does to correct inputs. Then I'd take the model out of anything after approval and copy the approved text exactly. Where the model helps, I'd move it before the person decides: suggest, show the changed letters, and let them accept or reject each line. A bigger model, a firm instruction and a sureness cut-off each made the failures rarer, never zero, and left them silent; staff checking every output works but doubles the checking. One wrong name loses more trust than many fixed typos earn.

An interview round on judging what a product should do and whether AI should do it at all, such as 'when would you not use a language model?'
Doing the same thing every time, so people can rely on it. Google's People + AI Guidebook lists it among cases where AI is probably not better.

atWork: Look for a model that runs after a person's approval and changes what they approved before it reaches anyone: a common pattern wherever a tidy, polish or clean-up step sits between a yes and the printer, the label maker or the send button. The first sign is usually a test that counts only fixes. Ask four things. After approval, is there one right answer? What does the step do to correct inputs, counted with the denominator, including rare names and unusual words? Who sees each change before it takes effect? And could the same help be offered as a suggestion, before the person decides? Dead Letter's s9e11 asks which service to run; this case asks whether a model belongs in the path at all. Build Night: this case feeds no milestone; the season finale, ai09, asks its question, whether AI should do the job at all. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 42001:2023 or working toward it, an AI step added to a live process is likely to need an impact assessment and verification before release, and a test that counts only fixes would not show its impact on correct inputs; check the clauses in your own copy. Where a SOC 2 report covers processing integrity (PI1), output that differs from the approved input with no record of why is the kind of gap an auditor is likely to look for. Neither note is legal advice.

cards.title: When AI is the wrong tool

recall.prompt: A school's report system lets each teacher write a comment for every pupil, and the head reads and approves them. Then a language model polishes the approved comments before they are printed. In its test, 100 comments with 10 grammar slips, it fixed 9. The head asks if it's safe. What do you check, and where should the model sit?

keyIdeas.idea: Count what it does to the correct comments too, with the denominator: of the 90 correct ones, how many changed
After approval there is one right answer: print the approved text exactly, with no model in between
Move it before approval as suggestions with the changes shown, and the teacher or head accepts or rejects each

recall.model: First I'd ask for the other half of the test: 9 of 10 slips fixed says nothing about the 90 correct comments, so I'd count how many correct ones it changed, out of 90, and include comments with unusual names and words. Then I'd point out that after the head approves, there is one right answer: print the approved text exactly. A model that writes likely text can only match it or drift from it, so no model after approval. If the polishing helps, move it before approval as suggestions, with the changes highlighted, and let the teacher accept or reject each one.

recall.prompt: On the club's list of 120 lines, 3 had typos and 117 were correct. The tidy step changed 9 lines: the 3 typos and 6 correct names. What share of the correct lines did it change?
recall.why: The question is about the correct lines, so the denominator is the 117 correct ones: 6 of 117 were changed. 9 of 120 counts every change, the 3 typo fixes included, and 6 of 9 only says how many of the changes were wrong.

recall.prompt: In a product sense round the interviewer asks: 'When would you not use a language model? Give an example.' How do you answer?

keyIdeas.idea: When the job has one known right answer that must be copied exactly
A model writes likely text, so a rare but correct input looks like an error to it
Where errors are costly and predictability matters, let the model suggest and show its changes, and a person decides

recall.model: I wouldn't use one where the job has one known right answer that must be copied exactly and a wrong one is costly. An engraving shop ran a model on customers' approved plate text: it fixed 14 of 15 typos in its test, but on one club's list it changed 6 of 117 correct names into commoner spellings, because a model writes likely text and a rare name looks like a typo to it. Predictability mattered more than a few fixed typos. Where a model still helps, I'd have it suggest before the person approves, show what it changed, and let the person decide line by line, and I'd measure it with denominators, including what it does to correct inputs.

recall.prompt: After the night, which change stops the tidy step altering approved text without anyone seeing it?
options: A bigger model that knows more names
'Never change names' added to its instructions
Changing only what it is 90% sure of
The approved text engraved exactly, tidy-ups offered before the proof
recall.why: Only taking the model out of the path after approval stops silent changes. In the sim the bigger model still changed 3 of 117 names, the instruction 2 and the 90% sure rule 4, each without anyone seeing. Before the proof, the 9 changes become suggestions the customer accepts or rejects, and 120 of 120 plates match.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Since Monday 14 December the tidy step runs before the proof: its suggestions go to the customer with the changed letters highlighted, one accept or reject per line, and the machine cuts the approved text exactly. In February customers asked for something quicker, so I added an 'accept all' button. On Wednesday 10 March a dance school's list of 64 plates came back with all 8 suggestions accepted in 11 seconds: 6 typo fixes, and 2 dancers' names changed to commoner spellings. The plates match the approved proof exactly. Both names are wrong, and the school has asked who changed them.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why are two names wrong on plates that match the approved proof, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: 'Accept all' made approval a reflex: 8 suggestions accepted in 11 seconds were not read, which is approval fatigue
Remove 'accept all': one decision per line, with the customer's own text kept unless they choose the change
Treat names differently: don't suggest changes to names; at most flag a spelling for the customer to confirm

coldCase.model: The plates are exactly what was approved; the approval itself went wrong. 8 suggestions accepted in 11 seconds means nobody read them: the accept all button turned each yes into a reflex, approval fatigue, so the 2 name changes became silent changes with the school's signature. Remove the accept all button and ask line by line, with the customer's own text kept by default unless they pick the change. And treat names differently: never suggest a change to a name; at most flag it and ask them to confirm the spelling, keeping what they typed. Then tell the school what happened and cut the two plates again from the spelling the school typed.
